claims.claim: A machine learning model learns from its training data, the set of examples it is shown while being trained, and improves its predictions through that process.
The test set is a separate portion of the dataset, set aside before training, used to check the trained model on cases it never saw; testing against unseen data is standard machine learning practice.
Testing a model on examples different from those it trained on is stronger proof of its quality than testing on the same examples.
A model evaluated on its own training data can look better than it really is, because it has already seen those examples; memorization can masquerade as learning.
The general practice is to set aside part of the data before training (ideally by a randomized split) and reserve it exclusively for testing after training finishes.
A test set loses value with repeated use: the more a team tunes the model based on test results, the more the model fits the test set and the less the results say about real-world performance.
Overfitting is the failure mode in which a model fits its training data so closely, memorizing even its noise, that it cannot make accurate predictions on new data.
A low error rate on the training data combined with a high error rate on the test data signals overfitting, which is why a test set is set aside to check for it.
Accuracy is the proportion of predictions that were correct, and it can mislead when one category dominates the data; errors are the predictions that missed.
Training is an iterative loop of training, evaluating, and refining, which is why evaluation of a model under development uses data other than the final test set.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a dataset should be split into two sets (train/test) or three sets (train/validation/test).
positions: A simple two-way split into training and test data is enough to explain the core idea at literacy level.
Google's ML Crash Course recommends a three-way split, with a validation set used during development so the test set stays fresh for the final check.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the two-set core and notes that careful teams use other data, such as a validation set, while still making changes, so the test set is used once at the end. Full validation-set workflow belongs to practitioner material, not this literacy lesson.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether accuracy is a good measure of a model.
positions: Accuracy is intuitive and the default summary for many models.
Accuracy alone can mislead, especially on imbalanced data where one category dominates.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names accuracy and errors simply and explicitly warns that one accuracy number is not the whole story, pointing to the evaluating-ai-output sibling topic for full metrics.

sourceRecords.title: Datasets: Dividing the original dataset (Machine Learning Crash Course)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21 at the canonical URL (the page was also reachable via /crash-course/training-and-test-sets/video-lecture, which redirects to the canonical path). Supports: models should be tested against a separate dataset called the test set to ensure accurate predictions on unseen data; the training set is what the model trains on; testing on different examples is stronger proof of fitness than testing on the same set; repeated use of a test set makes the model fit it ('teaching to the test'); test sets and validation sets wear out with repeated use and should be refreshed; duplicates between training and test sets undermine test results. Facts synthesized into original prose; no page wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: What is Overfitting?
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21. Supports: overfitting as a model fitting too closely or exactly to its training data so it cannot make accurate predictions on other data; the model memorizing noise within the dataset and failing to generalize; the standard practice that part of the data is typically set aside as a test set to check for overfitting; a low training error combined with a high test error signaling overfitting. Used only as a pointer for the failure-mode mention; the overfitting sibling topic owns the full treatment. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
